question: Can a single machine-learning primitive based on one ordered eigenvalue of an affine symmetric matrix pencil offer scalable expressivity, exact shape constraints, and parameter-level feature-influence information while remaining trainable with standard tools?

key_findings.claim: A spectral neuron maps scalar features to an affine symmetric matrix and reads one ordered eigenvalue, placing explicit matrix structure between a linear model and an opaque multilayer network.
key_findings.evidence: The model is f_k(x)=lambda_k(A_0+sum_i x_i A_i), with symmetric learned coefficient matrices and eigenvalue index k as its structural hyperparameter. The author explicitly identifies it as the affine-pencil, single-eigenvalue special case of the earlier Parametric Matrix Model framework rather than claiming the underlying construction is new.

key_findings.claim: Each coefficient matrix provides a certified global feature-sensitivity bound, with a tighter eigenspace-dependent local bound for a specific prediction.
key_findings.evidence: Eigenvalue perturbation gives |f_k(x+delta)-f_k(x)| <= sum_i |delta_i| ||A_i||_2, so ||A_i||_2 bounds output change per unit feature change globally. At x, if V spans the full eigenspace of lambda_k(A(x)), every Clarke subgradient component is bounded by ||V^T A_i V||_2; for a simple eigenvalue this reduces to the signed derivative v^T A_i v.

key_findings.claim: The eigenvalue index controls broad shape and expressivity: extreme eigenvalues are convex or concave, while any fixed internal index is a universal approximator on compact domains as matrix size grows.
key_findings.evidence: Rayleigh-Ritz makes the smallest eigenvalue concave and the largest convex as functions of x, and prior spectrahedral regression proves universal approximation within those shape classes. The paper invokes the Parametric Matrix Model result that internal ordered eigenvalues of affine pencils approximate arbitrary continuous functions on compact sets. It also expresses each internal eigenvalue as a difference of two convex Ky Fan sums.

key_findings.claim: Positive- or negative-semidefinite coefficient matrices impose exact partial monotonicity without post-hoc checking.
key_findings.evidence: Eigenvalue monotonicity under Loewner order guarantees that f_k is nondecreasing in x_i when A_i is positive semidefinite and nonincreasing when it is negative semidefinite, for every ordered eigenvalue k. Selecting k=1 or d can combine monotonicity with concavity or convexity.

key_findings.claim: Orthogonal similarity is both a useful symmetry and a limit on literal coefficient interpretability.
key_findings.evidence: Conjugating every A_i by the same orthogonal matrix leaves all predictions invariant, so one coefficient matrix may be chosen diagonal without losing expressive power. The paper uses this to simplify one PSD monotone coefficient, but it also acknowledges that latent-skill interpretations are nonunique because many rotated coefficient systems represent the same function.

key_findings.claim: A theory-guided initialization avoids a low-expressivity invariant subspace and protects the target eigenvalue's gradient from small-gap instability.
key_findings.evidence: If all coefficient matrices are simultaneously diagonalizable, first-order optimizers keep them in that family and the model remains an order statistic of affine functions. The proposed initialization gives A_0 an isolated zero at eigenvalue k with neighbors at +/-1, adds small diagonal jitter to otherwise identity-like A_i to break commutation, and proves a target eigengap of at least 1/2 for bounded inputs. Davis-Kahan motivates the gap as a control on eigenprojector gradient sensitivity.

key_findings.claim: Synthetic scaling studies support the operational, rather than merely theoretical, increase in fitting capacity with matrix dimension.
key_findings.evidence: Across noisy and noiseless univariate and bivariate spline targets, low-dimensional loss curves plateau on more complex functions while larger matrices continue improving with samples. Monotone-by-construction variants learn monotone targets more sample-efficiently at smaller budgets; in bivariate experiments, dimension 15 fits the reported complexity-13 functions well while smaller dimensions flatten.

key_findings.claim: On two large tabular datasets, spectral neurons improve with dimension and reach the broad performance range of parameter-matched nonlinear baselines, but do not establish state of the art.
key_findings.evidence: On Criteo, linear models flatten while spectral neurons and factorization machines continue improving; spectral neurons scale more consistently with dimension. On HIGGS, spectral neurons improve with dimension and are described as in the same performance ballpark as MLPs, although MLPs with at least two hidden layers are slightly better. Models train on up to 2^28 Criteo or 2^26 HIGGS samples with checkpoint-specific learning-rate tuning.

key_findings.claim: The certified global influence bound is nonvacuous on one HIGGS perturbation test but becomes looser as matrix dimension grows.
key_findings.evidence: For random half-standard-deviation feature corruptions, the paper plots actual logit change divided by |delta| ||A_i||_2. Ratios are measurably above zero for trained models, demonstrating possible usefulness, but their distribution concentrates increasingly near zero at larger dimensions, motivating spectral-norm regularization.

method.core_idea: Use a single ordered eigenvalue of an input-affine symmetric matrix as a nonlinear tabular predictor, and exploit matrix-analysis theorems to make expressivity, shape, sensitivity, differentiation, and initialization explicit.
method.mechanism: Features linearly combine learned symmetric matrices; a standard eigensolver returns lambda_k and its eigenspace. Rayleigh-Ritz, Courant, Ky Fan, Weyl, Davis-Kahan, eigenvalue monotonicity, and Clarke subdifferentials derive shape and influence properties. Dense matrices are parameterized with off-diagonal 1/sqrt(2) scaling so vector Euclidean norm matches matrix Frobenius norm. A diagonal squareplus parameterization enforces one PSD coefficient. Initialization isolates the selected eigenvalue and adds small noncommuting jitter. Adam then trains mid-eigenvalue models on synthetic splines, Criteo, and HIGGS under sample-budget scaling protocols.
assumptions: Inputs enter only through an affine symmetric matrix pencil, and the scalar output is one fixed ordered eigenvalue.
Matrix dimension can grow enough to realize inherited universal-approximation results; the paper does not give finite-dimension approximation rates for general functions.
Coefficient matrices are meaningful through invariant quantities such as spectral norms and eigenspace restrictions, not through individual basis-dependent entries.
The input range is bounded or standardized well enough for the initialization eigengap guarantee; the proposed jitter uses the heuristic bound ||x||_infinity<=5.
Standard eigensolver subgradients and first-order optimization behave usefully around nonsimple eigenvalues and avoid the simultaneous-diagonalization trap in practice.
One monotone coefficient may be made diagonal using the shared orthogonal symmetry; multiple constrained coefficients generally require a richer PSD parameterization.
Parameter-matched MLP and factorization-machine comparisons are sufficient only to establish rough practical viability, not best-in-class tabular performance.

techniques.role: Converts scalar features into a structured latent symmetric operator whose selected eigenvalue supplies the nonlinearity.
Uses extremal index and coefficient definiteness to guarantee convexity, concavity, and featurewise monotonicity.
Bounds global prediction sensitivity to each feature by the norm of its learned coefficient matrix.
Projects each coefficient matrix into the active eigenspace to obtain signed derivatives or nonsmooth local bounds.
Uses shared conjugation invariance to diagonalize one coefficient and simplify a PSD monotonicity constraint.
Separates the target eigenvalue while perturbing coefficients enough to escape the simultaneously diagonalizable model class.
Scales off-diagonal parameters so Euclidean optimizer steps in the vector representation match Frobenius geometry.
Tunes learning rate at each checkpoint and tests whether larger matrix dimensions continue improving as more examples are processed.

evaluations.setting: Random noisy and noiseless univariate spline targets of increasing knot complexity
evaluations.metric: Test loss versus samples processed for several odd matrix dimensions
evaluations.result: Larger dimensions continue improving on complex functions after smaller models plateau; monotone parameterization improves early sample efficiency on monotone targets.
evaluations.baseline: Lower-dimensional unconstrained and monotone spectral neurons

evaluations.setting: Random bivariate tensor-product splines and functions monotone in one coordinate
evaluations.metric: Test loss versus samples processed and matrix dimension
evaluations.result: Dimension-15 models fit reported complexity-13 targets well while lower-dimensional curves flatten; shape-constrained and unconstrained models converge to similar loss at larger budgets on monotone targets.
evaluations.baseline: Unconstrained spectral neuron at matched dimension

evaluations.setting: Criteo Display Advertising Challenge, 45,840,617 rows, chronological 80/10/10 split
evaluations.metric: Binary cross-entropy versus up to 2^28 samples seen
evaluations.result: Spectral neurons keep improving after the linear model plateaus, benefit from treating numeric columns continuously, scale with matrix dimension, and fall in the same broad range as a parameter-matched factorization machine.
evaluations.baseline: Linear model and parameter-matched factorization machine

evaluations.setting: HIGGS, 11,000,000 rows, 28 standardized numerical features, random 80/10/10 split
evaluations.metric: Binary cross-entropy versus up to 2^26 samples seen
evaluations.result: Spectral neurons improve with dimension and nonlinear data budget; depth-2-or-more MLPs are slightly better, while performance remains in a similar broad range.
evaluations.baseline: Linear model and parameter-matched MLPs of depths 1-3

evaluations.setting: Last-checkpoint HIGGS models under random standardized single-feature perturbations
evaluations.metric: Actual absolute prediction change divided by the certified |delta| ||A_i||_2 bound
evaluations.result: The bound is not identically vacuous, but ratios move closer to zero as matrix dimension increases, indicating progressively looser certification.
evaluations.baseline: The theoretical upper bound ratio of 1

limitations: Author-stated: the spectral neuron is a special case already contained in Parametric Matrix Models; the contribution is the focused synthesis of shape, influence, initialization, and scaling properties.
Author-stated: dense eigenvalue computation costs O(d^3), with O(n d^2) coefficient storage/work, and is substantially more expensive than a linear model or ordinary scalar neuron.
Author-stated: the initialization and PSD parameterization are heuristics rather than an exhaustive or optimal design study.
Author-stated: only one diagonal PSD coefficient is tested; multiple semidefinite feature matrices need new representations and initialization methods.
Author-stated: influence-bound usefulness is tested on HIGGS only and visibly worsens with dimension.

Reviewer-identified: shared orthogonal conjugation makes coefficient entries and latent-skill stories nonidentifiable, so 'coefficient transparency' is weaker than the unique scalar coefficients of a linear model.

Reviewer-identified: spectral norms are robustness certificates, not explanations of causal or semantic feature importance; no human, regulator, faithfulness, or decision-usefulness study validates the interpretability claim.
Reviewer-identified: real-data comparisons omit strong gradient-boosted-tree and modern tabular-model baselines and provide only two datasets, so the practical performance position is underspecified.
Reviewer-identified: exact monotonicity is demonstrated on synthetic targets, not on a real constrained application where violations and utility tradeoffs can be measured.
Reviewer-identified: nonsmooth eigenvalue crossings can destabilize autograd and attribution, while the empirical frequency and consequences of small gaps after initialization are not reported.
Reviewer-identified: inherited universal approximation establishes existence as d grows but does not establish sample complexity, approximation rates, or trainability of the required representations.
failure_modes: If coefficient matrices become simultaneously diagonalizable, gradient-based training can remain trapped in the lower-expressivity order-statistic-of-affine-functions family.
A small eigengap makes the active eigenprojector and parameter gradient highly sensitive to small matrix updates.
Repeated eigenvalues make local signed attribution set-valued; the bound may be much less informative than a unique derivative.
Large matrix dimension raises cubic compute while global influence certificates become increasingly loose.
A diagonal parameterization for several monotone features forces a shared eigenbasis and can sacrifice expressivity.
Feature values outside the assumed initialization range can close the protected eigengap before learning begins.
Orthogonally equivalent parameters can support conflicting coefficient-entry narratives even though predictions and invariant norms are identical.
On high-dimensional sparse tables, O(n d^2) parameters and dense eigensolves may eliminate the deployment advantage of a transparent single model.
reusable_insights: A classical numerical primitive can serve as a learnable nonlinearity when its variational, perturbation, and order properties yield guarantees unavailable to generic activations.
Separate basis-invariant interpretability claims from parameter-entry narratives whenever a model has a gauge symmetry.
Global robustness certificates and local active-subspace derivatives provide complementary levels of feature influence.
Check whether initialization lies in a gradient-invariant low-expressivity subfamily, not only whether its variance is well scaled.
Eigengap is an optimizer-conditioning variable because eigenvalue gradients are eigenprojectors whose sensitivity scales inversely with the gap.
Exact shape constraints can be encoded by cone membership of coefficients, making validity independent of sample coverage.
A scaling claim should be tested jointly against data budget and capacity; existence of a universal approximation theorem does not show that optimization reaches the richer functions.
Track how certification tightness changes with capacity, because more expressive models can retain a correct but operationally useless bound.
open_questions: Can tridiagonal, low-rank-plus-diagonal, sparse, or iterative eigensolver variants preserve most expressivity and guarantees with subcubic cost?
What initialization best maintains useful eigengaps throughout training without suppressing expressivity?
How should multiple PSD/NSD coefficients be parameterized without forcing a shared diagonal basis?
Do spectral neurons remain competitive against boosted trees and state-of-the-art tabular foundation or deep models across broad benchmark suites?
Can invariant matrix summaries support explanations that humans actually understand and use correctly despite orthogonal nonidentifiability?
Which spectral-norm or group penalties yield sparse feature selection while preserving predictive performance?
Can the proposed monotone spectral transform improve normalizing flows in practice, including stable and efficient inversion?
What finite-dimension approximation and sample-complexity rates connect target function structure to required matrix size?
How often do eigenvalue multiplicities and gap collapses occur during real training, and how should optimizers respond?

competitive_landscape.title: Parametric Matrix Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Parametric Matrix Models already define and prove universality for broad learned matrix-equation models, including affine pencils with eigenvalue readouts. The spectral-neuron paper's novelty is therefore the systematic study of one special case's ordered-eigenvalue shape guarantees, invariant influence bounds, initialization, and tabular scaling—not the core architecture.

competitive_landscape.title: Spectrahedral Regression
competitive_landscape.difference: Spectrahedral regression fits the maximum eigenvalue of an affine matrix pencil, proves convex approximation/risk bounds, and analyzes alternating minimization. The present paper covers every ordered eigenvalue, including universal nonconvex internal indices, and adds monotonicity, feature-sensitivity bounds, and standard-autograd experiments.

competitive_landscape.title: Input Convex Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: ICNNs make potentially deep networks convex in selected inputs and develop specialized inference and learning. An extremal spectral neuron obtains convexity from one eigenvalue of one matrix pencil and exposes coefficient norms, but pays dense eigensolver cost and has much less empirical validation.

competitive_landscape.title: Deep Lattice Networks and Partial Monotonic Functions
competitive_landscape.difference: Deep lattice networks guarantee partial monotonicity using constrained calibrators, lattices, and embeddings and report strong real-world results. The spectral neuron encodes monotonicity more compactly through PSD coefficients and supports arbitrary feature interactions, but does not establish comparable benchmark performance or deployment maturity.

competitive_landscape.title: Neural Additive Models: Interpretable Machine Learning with Neural Nets
competitive_landscape.difference: NAMs expose one learned scalar shape function per feature, giving directly visualizable additive effects but restricting interactions. Spectral neurons allow dense interactions and provide norm/eigenspace bounds, yet their matrix coefficients are basis-nonidentifiable and less immediately human-readable.

competitive_landscape.title: Maxout Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: When all coefficient matrices commute, the largest-eigenvalue spectral neuron reduces to a maxout unit and other indices become order-statistic units. Noncommuting matrices are the source of the proposed model's additional smooth spectral interactions and motivate its initialization.

novelty_assessment: Author claim: the contribution is a unified treatment of the spectral neuron as a practical machine-learning primitive combining capacity scaling, coefficient transparency, shape constraints, and feature-influence bounds. Reviewer inference after comparison: the architecture and universality are substantially inherited from Parametric Matrix Models, and the extremal case is already spectrahedral regression; convex, monotone, and interpretable tabular alternatives are mature. The defensible novelty is the ordered-eigenvalue specialization across internal indices, the local/global invariant influence analysis, the noncommuting eigengap initialization, and the initial scaling evidence. Calling its matrices as transparent as linear coefficients is too strong without human validation because the parameters are orthogonally nonidentifiable and the main invariant quantities are bounds rather than direct additive effects.
reviewer_notes: Read all 32 extracted pages, including mathematical properties, nonsmooth differentiation, initialization proof, compute accounting, complete experiment protocol, and discussion. The experimental figures do not print all numeric losses in extracted text, so results are reported qualitatively rather than reconstructed from pixels. Primary comparison records were checked on arXiv/OpenReview. Interpretability and benchmark-position caveats are reviewer inference.
